segments.say: Everything we built yesterday, we built while approving things. The tree on the left is everything yesterday produced — src, tests, tools, a CLAUDE dot md and a plan dot md, every one of them still marked U for untracked. Every file write, every command, one at a time. So the first question of today is the obvious one: what did all that approving actually buy us? I am asking it to count the times it had to stop and ask me for permission while building this project — and to say honestly which of those pauses were protecting something real, and which were just friction. Because there is a real trade here, and most people never think about it properly. Every prompt you answer is a moment where you could have caught something. It is also a moment where the work stops dead waiting for you. Get that balance wrong in one direction and you supervise nothing; get it wrong in the other and the agent is only as fast as your attention span. And it is worth being precise about what a permission prompt is actually for, because it is not one thing. Some of them are asking you to authorise something irreversible, and those are worth every second. Most of them are asking you to authorise reading a file, and those are asking you to be a rubber stamp. The skill is not answering them faster. It is arranging your work so that most of them never need to be asked, and the ones that are asked are the ones you would actually have stopped.

And it refuses. I cannot give you that count, and I do not want to invent one. Look at the line above the answer, though: ran two shell commands. It went and looked before it said no. Twenty-six seconds of checking, and the output of that checking is the refusal. An instant I do not know would have been worth nothing; this one costs something and therefore means something. It also names the four things it can see were built — src, tests, tools and plan dot md — so you know its blindness is about the transcript, not about the repo. It cannot see the sessions. It can see the result of them. Then it explains precisely why, and every reason is checkable. This conversation began with my question, so it has no transcript of the sessions that built the simulator. And nothing on disk recorded those pauses either: the memory folder is empty, there are no commits, and there is no local permissions file — which is the place a yes, and do not ask me again would have left a trace. So there is no record of a single permission prompt, let alone a count of them. And notice how specific the refusal is. It does not say I am not sure. It names the three places the evidence would be if it existed, and reports that each of them is empty. That is the difference between hedging and checking. A hedge protects the speaker. A check gives you somewhere to go next.

What it can see, it tells me instead. Our hook runs after every write, and that one never asks anybody anything — it blocks or it warns, automatically. The hook it names is a real file, check-content, sitting in our own tools folder and wired to run after every edit or write. That is the shape of a guardrail that costs you nothing at runtime. It has an opinion, it applies it to every write, and it never interrupts you to ask whether you meant it. And because no allowlist was ever created, whatever prompts did happen were answered individually and left nothing behind. Then it offers the honest route to a real answer. The raw session transcripts are on disk. They are JSONL, one line per event, under a projects folder keyed to this repo's path. Everything an agent did on your machine is already written down in plain text. Most people never open it. It can read them and give me an actual count, with the specific tool call behind every single pause. Say the word. And then the line I would put in front of anybody learning to work this way. Had I answered from vibes, you would have got a confident number with a tidy retrospective attached... and no way to tell that it was fabricated. That failure mode is worth more caution than most of the permission prompts themselves. Sit with that, because it is the actual job of the person in your chair. Not typing. Knowing the difference between an answer and a plausible answer. There is also a practical lesson hiding in that empty permissions file, and it is worth taking now rather than after you need it. If you never say yes and do not ask again, you never build up a record of what you decided was safe. Every session starts from nothing and asks you the same questions again. The allowlist is not a convenience feature. It is the memory of your own judgement, and an empty one means yesterday's thinking has to be done again today.

So we get to the real question of the day. If approving everything is slow, what can we safely stop approving? I ask it to explain the sandbox built into this version: what it stops, what it does not stop, and the specific case where it is not enough. And to show me how to turn it on for this project. What is on screen while it works on that is not a documentation page. It is a shell loop running strings over the installed binary itself, version two point one point two five one, hunting for the setting names the program actually knows about. Six commands deep before a single word of answer. Notice the shape of that question. Not tell me about sandboxing. Tell me where it fails. Because the honest version of speeding up is not bravery. It is knowing exactly which risks you have removed and which ones you have simply stopped being told about. Those are not the same thing, and a lot of people who say they run in YOLO mode have only done the second one. And there is a second reason to ask where it fails rather than what it does. Anything that describes itself is going to describe itself well. The limitations page is the part nobody writes for marketing, so it is the part that tells you what you are actually buying. If you only read one page about a safety feature, read that one.

And watch how it answers, because this is the part that matters. It does not tell me from memory. It goes and looks — first at the settings the installed binary itself understands, pulled straight out of the program on this machine, then at the current documentation, including the page headed limitations. That is the difference between an agent that recalls a feature and one that checks it. These tools change every few weeks. A confident answer from memory is worth very little, and this is the second time in one lecture it has chosen to go and verify rather than sound sure. You can see both fetches land. The first URL comes back a redirect, nine hundred and sixty bytes; the second returns seventy kilobytes, and it immediately runs a sed to pull the lines under the heading LIMITATIONS out of the middle of it. Not the whole page. The one section that says what does not work. Which, as it happens, is exactly the standard we are about to apply to ourselves. Because in the next lecture we stop asking the agent for permission altogether — and the only reason that is safe is that we will have checked, properly, what the walls are actually made of. One more thing worth taking from this lecture before we move. Twice now, asked a direct question, it chose to say I do not know and here is how we could find out. That is not the behaviour people expect from these tools, and it is the behaviour you should be selecting for. An agent that is confidently wrong costs you far more than one that is slow. You can plan around slow. And the answer it lands on is not a summary of the docs — it finds a hole in our own setup. Hooks run outside the sandbox, and our content hook sits under tools rather than under the protected dot claude folder. So a sandboxed command could rewrite the script that enforces our own rules, and that rewrite would run unsandboxed. Moving one file into the protected folder closes it. The limitation it found was ours, not the product's. A sandbox you have not read the exceptions to is a feeling, not a boundary. Watch the pattern across the whole lecture, because it is the pattern to select for. Asked to count something it had no record of, it said so. Asked to describe a feature, it read the binary on this machine and then the current page rather than reciting what it remembered. Neither of those is impressive on its own. Together they are the only reason the next lecture is safe to attempt at all.
